10924-the-lands-of-the-saracen-pictures-:
Bayard Taylor travelled for nearly two and a half years in the 1850s and published this volume on Palestine, Syria, Asia Minor, Sicily, and Spain. Dedicated to Washington Irving, whose writings on the Saracens inspired him, the book gathers letters written on the road, revised for print. Taylor had meant to spend one winter in Africa; instead his wanderings grew into three journeys.

Readers cross the Cilician plain with Kurdish hosts, pass marble fragments of ancient towns, and climb toward snow-tipped peaks, then move on to Spanish scenes Irving had already made famous. Taylor claims only sincerity and personal impression, not learned history. The result is a vivid mid-Victorian travel book, curious about Eastern life and frank about the discomforts of the road.
13471-letters-of-ulysses-s-grant-to-his-:
Jesse Grant Cramer edits letters from Ulysses S. Grant to his father and youngest sister, covering 1857 to 1878, with portraits of Grant, his father Jesse Root Grant, and his mother Hannah Grant. A facsimile letter and Grant's proclamation to the citizens of Paducah open the volume.

Grant writes on campaigns, commanders, and home. Prentiss, leaving Jackson for St. Louis offended at serving under a junior brigadier, made a great mistake, Grant says long after, though no man was braver or more sincere in devotion to the cause. Later letters send orders for a mail messenger, report excellent health, and long for respite and a summer visit home. The letters show a general in family voice.
14047-a-letter-to-a-h-esq-concerning-the:
The Augustan Reprint Society reprinted two 1698 essays on the stage in 1946, with an introduction by H. T. Swedenberg Jr. A Letter to A. H. Esq. Concerning the Stage and The Occasional Paper number nine form series three, essays on the stage, number one. Swedenberg, with Hooker and Boys, founded the society in 1946.

The essays debate stage morality, with clergy in black coats as a target. Drunkenness, whoring, insolence, and dulness on stage, the writer argues, forced real clergy to keep within bounds. The reprint, priced seventy-five cents, drew on California library collections. It suits students of Restoration theatre. The essays show early attacks on the stage.
1592-the-greatest-english-classic-a-stud:
Cleland Boyd McAfee studies the King James Bible as the greatest English classic, asking why its language shaped English prose, poetry, and speech. The book traces the translation's history and its literary power. McAfee, a Presbyterian minister and scholar, wrote for church readers and students.

McAfee weighs the translators' choices, the rhythm of the text, and its place in worship and reading. Readers of the Bible as literature will find here a clear, admiring study of a book that became a nation's voice. The King James Version of 1611, made by committees of scholars, shaped English for centuries.
16537-myths-that-every-child-should-know:
Hamilton Wright Mabie edited this 1906 collection of classic myths for young people, with pictures by Blanche Ostertag. Hawthorne's Wonder Book and Tanglewood Tales supply the golden apples, pomegranate seeds, Chimaera, golden touch, Gorgon's head, and dragon's teeth. Church's Homer, Kingsley's Greek Heroes, and Norse tales of Odin and giants follow.

Mabie gathered the stories with permission from their publishers, shaping a first mythology for children. The retellings are clear and vivid, with heroes, monsters, and gods in full color. Families seeking a first book of myths will find this old anthology still fresh and well chosen.
18787-life-of-st-francis-of-assisi:
Paul Sabatier's life of St. Francis of Assisi, translated by Louise Seymour Houghton and published by Hodder and Stoughton in 1919, follows the saint from youth to death. Sabatier writes to friends at Strasbourg, confessing his long delay and his days lost dreaming at Florence, Assisi, and Rome.

Chapters trace Francis's conversion, the church of 1209, his meeting with Innocent III, Rivo-Torto, Portiuncula, and Santa Clara. Later chapters treat the crisis of the order, the rule of 1221, the stigmata, the Canticle of the Sun, and his last year, will, and death. A critical study of the sources and an appendix on the stigmata close a book that helped revive the study of the Middle Ages.
19231-the-mummy-and-miss-nitocris-a-phan:
George Griffith wrote this fantasy, The Mummy and Miss Nitocris, a phantasy of the fourth dimension, reprinted by Arno Press in 1976 from an older edition. A professor puzzles over N to the fourth, while his daughter Niti pours whisky through a jar that seems to occupy the same space as her hand. Two bodies in one place defy accepted axioms.

The professor, fearing a headache before his Institute address, tries to stay calm as his daughter, unaware, serves his drink through solid matter. A mummy, an Egyptian queen, and fourth-dimensional wonders follow. Readers get a wild Victorian occult fantasy of science, ghosts, and hidden dimensions.
4543-the-querist-containing-several-quer:
George Berkeley, spelled Berkley in this edition, published The Querist in 1735 as a string of questions put to the public, not as a set of answers. He asks whether an industrious nation was ever poor, or an idle one rich, and whether a people can be called poor when the common sort are well fed, clothed, and lodged. He presses readers on the drift of a wise state, the true source of wealth in labour and the four elements, and the use of money.

Later queries ask whether money is useful only so far as it stirs industry, whether other means could excite industry just as well, and whether the real aim of men is power. Berkeley writes for Ireland and any state worried about trade and work. Readers get a sharp work of economic thought, best read slowly, question by question. Each query invites argument rather than assent.
6367-the-life-and-legends-of-saint-franc:
Father Candide Chalippe's life of Saint Francis, translated from French and revised by Father Hilarion Duerk, opens in a jubilee edition dedicated to Third Order members in Cleveland. Five books trace Francis from birth and prediction of greatness through studies, commerce, purity, and love for the poor, to prison, sickness, and a mysterious dream. He wishes for war, Christ dissuades him, and a crucified apparition changes his course.

Francis kisses a leper, goes to Rome, mingles with the poor, and hears a voice commanding him to restore the church of Saint Damian. He sells cloth from his father's house, escapes his father's anger, and returns to Assisi ill treated and confined, until his mother frees him. Later, a man at San Saloni promises hospitality to all Friars Minor passing through, and Francis names him father of the order. The book is legend as devotion, told with care.
8315-the-bible-douay-rheims-book-15-1-es:
Cyrus of Persia lets the exiles go home, and this book follows them back to Jerusalem. Named 1 Esdras in the Douay-Rheims Bible, it is the book of Ezra. It tells of rebuilding the temple against local opposition, reading the law, and Ezra's stern reforms, including the sending away of foreign wives. The story moves between royal decrees and the hard work of a small returned community.

Challoner's revision of the Vulgate text gives the book its older Catholic form, with Esdras for Ezra. Readers meet a people trying to stay distinct after disaster, rebuilding walls, altar, and identity at once. It pairs naturally with Nehemiah, which tells the next chapter of the same return.
8316-the-bible-douay-rheims-book-16-2-es:
Nehemiah's own voice drives this book, known in the Douay-Rheims Bible as 2 Esdras. A cupbearer to the Persian king hears that Jerusalem's walls lie broken, gets leave to return, and rebuilds the wall in fifty-two days despite threats and ridicule. Lists of builders, gate by gate, give way to a great public reading of the law, with the people weeping and then feasting.

The book closes with reforms: debts forgiven, sabbaths guarded, and marriages with outsiders broken up, measures that trouble modern readers. Challoner's Vulgate-based wording gives Nehemiah's memoir its older Catholic form. Paired with 1 Esdras, it tells the full story of a community rebuilding city, law, and identity after exile.
8322-the-bible-douay-rheims-book-22-prov:
Short sayings for living well fill Proverbs, the wisdom book linked to Solomon. A father warns his son against folly, pictured as a loud woman in the streets, and commends wisdom, pictured as a lady calling at the gates. Honest scales, guarded tongues, hard work, and respect for parents recur in paired lines built to stick in memory.

Later chapters collect sayings of other sages and close with praise of a capable wife who buys fields, runs a household, and speaks with wisdom. The Douay-Rheims text, in Challoner's revision from the Vulgate, keeps the older phrasing of these familiar lines. Readers dip into Proverbs for one saying at a time, as a handbook of conduct rather than a book to read straight through.
8328-the-bible-douay-rheims-book-28-jere:
Jeremias is the Douay-Rheims name for Jeremiah, prophet of Jerusalem's last days. Called young, he warned kings and crowds that injustice and idol worship would bring Babylon down on the city, and he paid for it with mockery, beatings, and a pit of mud. His confessions, where he argues with God and curses the day he was born, make this the most personal prophetic book.

Sermons, acted signs, letters to exiles, and the fall of Jerusalem itself fill the long text, which ends with hope: a new covenant written on hearts. Challoner's revision from the Vulgate keeps the older spelling and the book's raw edge. Readers meet a prophet who suffered for a message he could not keep silent.
8331-the-bible-douay-rheims-book-31-ezec:
Ezechiel is the Douay-Rheims spelling of Ezekiel, the priest-prophet carried to Babylon. His book opens with a storm vision of living creatures and wheels. It then moves through acted parables, oracles against Jerusalem and its neighbors, and the famous valley of dry bones, where scattered bones rise and breathe. A final vision measures a new temple in exact detail.

Challoner's Vulgate-based English gives the visions their older Catholic wording, and the book's strangeness has lost none of its force. Ezekiel speaks to exiles who have lost land, temple, and king, and promises new hearts and a gathered people. Artists and preachers have returned to the dry bones ever since, as an image of hope after ruin.
8666-security-in-your-old-age-to-employe:
The Social Security Board issued this 1936 pamphlet for employees of factories, shops, mines, mills, stores, offices, and other businesses. Beginning November 24, 1936, the United States government would set up a Social Security account for each eligible worker, and the pamphlet explains, in plain language, their obligations, rights, and benefits. About twenty-six million working people, it says, would gain something to live on when old and no longer working.

The leaflet walks a worker through the new law, called the Social Security Act, without legal jargon: who counts, what the account means, and what to do next. As a historical document it captures the New Deal speaking directly to ordinary wage earners at the moment a new safety net began. Readers today get both a clear summary of the original system and a glimpse of how the government first explained old-age insurance to the public.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anglona-tursi:
The Italian diocese of Anglona-Tursi, in the Archdiocese of Acerenza, covers twenty-seven towns and three villages in Potenza province. Nine towns and one village in Cosenza province complete it. It is sometimes called Tursi alone, because Anglona's see moved to that city after Anglona's destruction in Queen Johanna of Naples's days.

History mentions the Diocese of Anglona very late, and all knowledge of its origin and church organization is lost in the Middle Ages. The first Bishop of Anglona found, Simon, appears in 1077. He was present at Hugo di Chiaromonte and his wife Ginarga's donation of some fields to the celebrated Basilian monastery of Saints Elias and Anastasius. The diocese counts 40 parishes, with 138 secular priests serving 95,000 inhabitants.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antonio-franc:
Theatine priest and biographical writer Antonio Francesco Vezzosi, born at Arezzo in 1708 and dead in Rome in 1783, gave his life to teaching and church scholarship. He entered the Theatine Congregation, a clerical order, in 1731, taught philosophy at Rimini, then theology at San Andrea della Valle in Rome from 1742. His fine learning and loyal orthodoxy, or sound doctrine, won him charge of editing the collected works of Cardinal Tommasi in eleven volumes between 1749 and 1769.

Pope Benedict XIV noticed the work and made him professor of church history at the Sapienza college in 1753, and examiner of candidates for bishop. He later became general, or head, of his congregation. His own publications include an oration praising Leo X and a two-volume lives of Theatine writers, published in 1780. Later writers used that work as the base for a Theatine library catalogue.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-assisi:
Assisi is a diocese in Umbria, Italy, whose town takes its name from Mount Asi, where it stands, almost in Umbria's centre. It stands halfway between Perugia and Foligno and some forty-one miles north of Rome. Assisi's beginnings are obscure, but in early imperial times it had grown into a flourishing municipality of some importance. It claimed, with some show of truth, to be the birthplace of the Latin poet Propertius.

The gospel was first preached to Assisians about the mid-third century by Cyspolitus, bishop of Bettona, martyred under Emperor Maximilian. About 235 Rufinus was named bishop of Assisi by Pope Fabian, suffered martyrdom about 236, and was followed by Victorinus. Both Victorinus and his successor Sabinus died martyrs. The entry sets a diocese famous for Francis, though its early bishops already fill a martyr's roll.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bernardo-de-r:
Bernardo de Rossi, a Dominican theologian and historian, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Cividale del Friuli in 1687, he died at Venice in 1775 after professing with the Dominicans at Conegliano in 1704 and studying at Florence and Venice. Fifteen years of teaching at Venice followed and twice served as vicar-general of his province.

In 1722 he went with a Venetian embassy to Louis XV as its theologian, spending five months in Paris. Resigning his chair in 1730, he gave the rest of a long life to writing, and his letters to the great men of his age fill nine volumes. Holiness and learning together won him a wide reputation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-aegidius-o:
Blessed Giles of Assisi, one of St. Francis's first companions, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Francis called him the knight of his round table, and he holds first place among the companions. His early life is obscure.

In April 1209, moved by two Assisians who had just joined Francis, Giles begged to join the little band and was clothed in a poor habit on St. George's feast. He preached with Francis in the Marches of Ancona and travelled with him to Rome. The entry presents a simple brother whose sayings became Franciscan wisdom.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-giuseppe-m:
Blessed Giuseppe Maria Tommasi, a cardinal famed for learning, humility, and reforming zeal, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Licata in Sicily in 1649 to a princely family, he died at Rome in 1713. Destined for the Spanish court, he instead joined the Theatines at Palermo in 1665, giving up his birthright to his brother.

Greek, Ethiopic, and Arabic joined philosophy and theology in his studies, and ordination came on Christmas Day 1673. His editions of ancient liturgical texts served the Church's prayer, and as cardinal he pressed reform with humility. The entry presents a prince turned scholar-priest.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-brindisi:
Brindisi, the Adriatic seaport the Romans called Brundusium, guarded Italy's road to the East from the Via Appia's end. Taken bloodlessly in 245 before Christ, it became a Roman colony and Caesar's naval base against Pompey. Pacuvius was born there, Virgil died there in 19 before Christ, and barbarian sackings never killed it: by the twelfth century it held 60,000 people.

Legend names Leucius bishop about 165, though Christianity likely reached it in the first century. Saracen ruin drove bishops to Oria in the tenth century, and Oria became its own diocese in 1591. Brindisi, an archbishopric since the tenth century, joined Ostuni in 1818. Roger II built its present cathedral in 1140, and its bishops include Aproculus, Cyprian, and Eustachio, first styled archbishop.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-conversi:
Stephen Donovan's entry defines conversi as lay brothers. Originally the term covered adults who renounced the world for penance and a better life. Renunciation was called conversio a sæculo, aiming at change of life, conversio morum, hence conversi, the converted. They differed from oblati, children offered by parents to a monastery for religious instruction and profane knowledge.

In the eleventh century Saint John Gualbert, founder of the Vallisumbrosani Benedictines, first distinguished lay brothers from priests or choir religious. Among conversi were often the illiterate, those who had led scandalous lives, or notorious criminals. Barring them from cloister penance seemed unjust, yet they hardly suited orders. Orders therefore received them for manual labour and sometimes temporal affairs. The same holds for women, though conversæ versus choir religious appears only from the twelfth century. Conversi wear a distinct habit, while vows and monastic life stay alike for all.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dominic-valla:
Dominic Vallarsi was an Italian priest born at Verona on 13 November 1702. He studied with the Jesuits there and, once ordained, gave himself to archaeology and the study of the fathers. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry tells how the city of Verona and its bishop, with Pope Benedict the Fourteenth, funded his hunts for manuscripts and antiquities. The pope gave him a benefice at Vicenza and made him reviser of Oriental tongues at the Holy Office.

Muratori, Zeno, and Mazzuchelli respected his learning, though his one fault was dogmatism and scant regard for the learning of others. His chief work is an edition of Saint Jerome, and he also aided Maffei on Saint Hilary and issued an incomplete Rufinus. He died at Verona in 1771, a scholar of the old Italian school.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eastern-kiang:
Eastern Kiang-Si is a vicariate apostolic in China, cut from Northern Kiang-Si in 1885. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry gives the mission eight million souls across four prefectures: Fu-chou-fu, Kien-chang-fu, Yao-chou-fu, and Kwang-sin-fu. Its first vicar apostolic, Casimir Vic, a Lazarist named titular bishop of Metellopolis in 1885, lived at Fu-chou-fu and still held the post when the entry was written.

The mission's seminary in 1899 held a bishop, sixteen Lazarists, six native priests, and sisters of two orders, with fifty-six schools, sixty-six churches, and ten orphanages. By 1908 it counted ninety-six churches, seventy-three schools, two hospitals, a leper house, and more than sixteen thousand Catholics with three thousand catechumens. The entry is a snapshot of a young mission growing fast.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-filippo-anfos:
Filippo Anfossi was an Italian Dominican born at Taggia, in the province of Genoa. He died at Rome on 14 May 1825, after serving as Master of the Sacred Palace from 1815. Pius VII had first made him vicar-general of the Preachers' order on returning to the States of the Church. In his Roman office he negotiated with Lamennais over corrections to the Essai sur l'indifférence.

He ranked among the Roman Church's most ardent defenders against Gallicanism in its several forms. His targets included Guillaume de la Luzerne, Scipione de Ricci, and Vincento Palmieri. His published works defended the bull Auctorem fidei and rejected the four Gallican propositions. A later work weighed the union of Church and state in its bearing on civil society.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fioretti-di-s:
The Fioretti, or Little Flowers, gather popular legends of St. Francis and his early companions. The book grew by slow stages and has no single author; it is in a sense a national work. Critics hold it a translation of a lost Latin original, the Actus of Francis and his companions. The first half retells early Franciscan tradition; the later chapters concern friars of the March of Ancona.

Fra Ugolino da Monte Giorgio is believed to have written much of the later part before 1328. Four appendixes on the Stigmata, Fra Ginepro, and Fra Egidio came from later hands. The Italian version, in limpid Tuscan, ranks among the masterpieces of Italian literature. The earliest known manuscript dates from 1390, and Vicenza first printed the work in 1476.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-galeazzo-ales:
Galeazzo Alessi, a famous Italian architect born in 1500, gave Genoa the splendid buildings behind its title La Superba, the Proud. Gifted early in mathematics and letters, he studied drawing under Caporali and befriended Michelangelo at Rome. He finished Perugia's fortress, built palaces there, and then spent years at Genoa laying streets, restoring walls, and raising churches.

His harbor design stands out: a great gate with rustic columns, a Doric portico on the sea front, and a mole stretched over 600 paces into the water. At Milan he built San Vittore and the Marini palace, at Bologna the gate of the public palace, and at Assisi he worked on the angels' church. His Escorial plan was judged best in Europe, but age kept him from building it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giambattista-:
Giambattista Piranesi was an Italian etcher and engraver born at Venice in 1720, who died at Rome in 1778. Sent to Rome in 1738, he studied architecture under Valeriani and engraving under Vasi, and in 1741 he issued a work on ancient arches, bridges, and remains. A Catholic Encyclopedia article calls him the Rembrandt of architecture for his dramatic black-and-white views of Roman ruins.

He drew straight onto copper and etched more than two thousand large plates, full of detail, vigor, and brilliance. His shadows glow, though at times the contrast runs too strong, and his ruins teem with small Callot-like figures. Twenty-nine folio volumes hold his Roman antiquities, views, statues, and vases. He also repaired churches in Rome, and his plates passed at last into the pope's hands.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gian-domenico:
Gian Domenico Mansi was an Italian prelate and scholar born at Lucca in 1692, who died as its archbishop in 1769. He entered the Congregation of Clerks Regular of the Mother of God at sixteen. He spent most of his life in his religious house. A Catholic Encyclopedia article calls him an indefatigable worker whose name stands on ninety folio volumes, though a savant rather than a strict critic.

His own chief work was a 1724 treatise on reserved cases and censures, which brought him trouble with the Index. The rest were annotated reprints, from Baronius's Annals in twenty-eight volumes to histories by Natalis Alexander and others. His best-known work remains the vast collection of church councils, begun in 1758 and carried to thirty-one volumes, though he lived to see only fourteen in print.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-batt:
Giovanni Battista de Rossi was a distinguished Christian archaeologist born at Rome in 1822, who died at Castel Gandolfo in 1894. Called the modern founder of Christian archaeology, he mastered secular archaeology, epigraphy, and the ancient and medieval topography of Rome. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a scholar whose work centered on the Roman catacombs.

In 1841, against his father's protests, he first visited a neglected catacomb under the guidance of the Jesuit Father Marchi. The two pursued the study together and planned a systematic collection of all Christian inscriptions. With his brother Michele Stefano as assistant, de Rossi explored the burial places and drew exact plans. He published his findings in Roma Sotterranea, and guided strangers of high rank through the underground world himself.

Giovanni Battista Pergolesi was a composer born at Naples in 1710, who died at Pozzuoli near Naples in 1736. Of frail build and delicate poetic gifts, he trained at the Conservatory dei poveri di Gesù Cristo, studying violin and composition. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a short life torn between the theater and the church.

Early theater pieces gave way to masses for thanksgiving after an earthquake, written for two five-part choirs and two orchestras. His intermezzo Serva padrona, for two singers and strings, won instant and lasting success. His last two years went almost wholly to liturgical texts. They were crowned by the Stabat mater for two-part choir, strings, and organ, written shortly before his death for the Minorites of Naples.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-doss:
Giovanni Dossi, really Giovanni di Nicolo di Lutero and called Dosso Dossi, was an Italian painter born about 1479, who died at Ferrara in 1542. Of the Ferrara school and a pupil of Lorenzo Costa at Mantua, he spent eleven years with his brother Battista at Rome and Venice, studying Giorgione and Titian. A Catholic Encyclopedia article presents a romantic colorist of imaginative power.

He and his brother served Alfonso I and Ercole II, dukes of Ferrara, and his greatest work is the altarpiece in the Ferrara Gallery. He painted tapestry cartoons for the cathedral and San Francesco, and frescoes in the ducal palace. His landscape backgrounds glow with beauty and imagination. His portrait of Ariosto earned the poet's praise in Orlando Furioso, ranking him with Leonardo, Michelangelo, Raphael, and Titian.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giuseppe-agos:
Giuseppe Agostino Orsi was a cardinal, theologian, and ecclesiastical historian born at Florence on 9 May 1692, who died at Rome on 12 June 1761. In secular life called Agostino Francesco, he entered the Dominican Order at Fiesole in 1708 and took the name Giuseppe Agostino at profession. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a scholar of the Fathers and the great Scholastics.

Called to Rome in 1732 as professor of theology at the college of Saint Thomas, he became theologian of Cardinal Neri Corsini. He served as secretary of the Congregation of the Index in 1738 and papal theologian in 1749. Clement XIII made him cardinal in 1759. His chief work, the twenty-volume Storia ecclesiastica of 1747 to 1761, reached only the close of the sixth century, and was carried to 1587 by later hands.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jesi:
Jesi, ancient Aesis, is a diocese in Ancona province, Italy, directly subject to the Holy See, set on a pleasant height beside the Esino River, boundary between Umbria and Piceno. Little survives of its ancient temples and baths, still standing in the fourteenth century.

After Lombard invasion Jesi joined the Pentapolis, later the March of Ancona, and in pope-emperor struggles it stood Ghibelline. Frederick II, born there, used it as his base. Saint Septimius, martyred in 307, counts as first bishop, with Florianus, Martianus, Calumniosus, and Honestus among early holy bishops. Bishop Severinus began a new cathedral in 1237, and later bishops rebuilt and reformed the see.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-baptist-:
John Baptist de Rossi was a Roman priest of the eighteenth century remembered as an apostle to the poor and outcast. Born at Voltaggio near Genoa in 1698, he was brought to Rome as a boy and studied at the Collegium Romanum under the Jesuits. He was ordained in 1721 despite spells of epilepsy brought on by excessive mortification. He vowed to accept no benefice unless obedience commanded it.

Instead he preached at dawn and dusk to laborers, herdsmen, and teamsters of the Campagna at the old Forum. He visited the sick and poor at the hospital of Saint Galla, and in 1731 founded a refuge there for wanderers of the night. Made canon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, he gave the house's rent to good purposes. Though fear of his sickness long kept him from the confessional, he sent penitents he had converted on to other priests.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kwangi-si:
Kwang-si is a prefecture apostolic covering a mountainous, very poor Chinese province of about ten million people, among them Canton settlers, Hakkas, and wild Yao-tse and Miao-tse peoples. Jesuit Father Ruggieri failed to settle at Kwei-lin in 1583.

Franciscans, Augustinians, and others followed: Father Koffler raised a church at Kwei-lin and baptized a Ming pretender's son as Constantine, and Father Boym worked beside him. All were expelled in 1724, and no missionary returned for 130 years. In 1854 Blessed Auguste Chapdelaine entered from Kwei-chou, was twice arrested, and was executed on 29 February 1856 with two companions. Pius IX raised Kwang-si to a prefecture apostolic on 6 August 1875.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lapsi:
Lapsi, from Latin labi, to slip, was the third-century name for Christians who fell back into heathenism. Above all it meant those who broke under persecution and denied the faith by sacrifice or other acts. Most, in the great persecutions after mid-century, did not return from conviction but lacked courage to confess when threatened with loss, banishment, forced labour, or death.

Confession under all circumstances and avoidance of any denial stood firm in the Church from apostolic times. Pliny notes true Christians would neither sacrifice nor revile Christ. Yet Hermas's Shepherd and martyrdom accounts show second-century weakness, and Trajan's rescript aimed precisely at apostasy, freeing those who performed pagan worship. Lyons in 177 saw ten brethren fall, several later returning through the steadfast prisoners' example and kindness.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-maria-gaetana:
Maria Gaetana Agnesi was an Italian woman of remarkable gifts, born at Milan in 1718 and dead there in 1799. Her father taught mathematics at Bologna. At nine she spoke Latin fluently and argued in a discourse that liberal studies suited her sex. At eleven she spoke Greek, and by thirteen she knew Hebrew, French, Spanish, German, and more, earning the name Walking Polyglot.

She disliked such displays and at twenty wished to enter a convent, but instead retired to study mathematics. Her Propositiones Philosophicae appeared in 1738, a treatise on conic sections followed, and her two-volume Instituzioni Analitiche of 1748 became the best guide to Euler's work, translated into English and French. The curve versiera bears her name as the Witch of Agnesi. Benedict XIV named her to teach mathematics at Bologna in 1750, and late in life she directed Milan's Trivulzio Hospice and joined the Blue Nuns.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marsi:
Marsi was a diocese in Aquila province, central Italy, seated at Pescina. Alone except Sabina, it took its name from a people, not a city. The warlike Marsi lived round Lake Fucino, allied with Rome in 325 B.C., revolted for Samnites in 309, and returned to Rome in 304.

Their chief goddess was Angitia. Under Lombards their land became a county of Spoleto, whose counts gave popes to the Church, among them Innocent III. Legend says St Mark preached to them in apostolic times, and Bishop St Rufinus was martyred about 240. The see began at Santa Savina, but Gregory XIII let it move to Pescina in 1580, its cathedral finished in 1596. Bishops included St Berardo, Montecassino pupil and cardinal, Jacopo in 1276, Angelo Maccafani in 1445, Marcello Crescenzi in 1533, and Gian Paolo Caccia in 1648, who aided public schools. The diocese, subject at once to the Holy See, held seventy-eight parishes and 146,000 people.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-matthew-of-ba:
Matthew of Bassi, born at Bascio in the Duchy of Urbino in 1495, founded the Capuchin branch of the Franciscans and served as its first superior-general. He joined the Observants at seventeen, and by 1525, troubled by laxity across the Franciscan family, he sought a sterner life in a habit closer to that of St. Francis. Pope Clement VII let him preach anywhere and take a companion, and others soon joined him.

The bull Religionis zelus of July 1528 gave the new reform formal standing, and the people's nickname for the hooded friars, Capuchin, stuck as the order's name. At Albacina in April 1529 the brethren chose Bassi vicar-general and drew up a rule. He soon stepped down to return to preaching across Italy and part of Germany, dying at Venice in 1552 amid a crowd drawn by his saintly fame.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-northern-kian:
Northern Kiang-Si, a vicariate apostolic in China, began when Matteo Ricci passed through the province near the end of the sixteenth century. Preaching on his way from Canton to the capital, Ricci planted the first seed, and seventeenth-century missionaries of several orders followed.

Innocent XII made the province a vicariate under Augustinian Alvares Benavento, who settled at Kan-chou-fu, while Jesuits built churches at Yao-chou and Nan-chang. Persecution, Lazarist care from 1838, and later growth fill a story the entry carries into the twentieth century. Father Entrecolles sent a study of Chinese moulding from King-te-chen in 1722.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-northern-shen:
Northern Shen-Si, a vicariate apostolic in northwest China, grew from a first preaching in 1640 through favor and disfavor at the imperial court. Attached to Shan-Si until 1841, Kan-su and Ku-Ku-Nor stayed with it until 1878, then split into northern and southern vicariates in 1887.

Franciscans run the mission across five prefectures around Si-ngan, where Bishop Maurice Gabriel resided after his 1908 consecration. By 1910 the vicariate counted 25,116 Catholics, 4,627 catechumens, and 203 churches and chapels before a further split in 1911. Its climate is healthful, though winters bite hard, and the mission counts five prefectures around Si-ngan.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pange-lingua-:
Pange Lingua Gloriosi opens two hymns, one for the Passion and one for the Blessed Sacrament. The Passion hymn, in unrhymed verse, is generally credited to Saint Venantius Fortunatus of the sixth century, while Saint Thomas Aquinas wrote the rhymed Sacrament hymn in the thirteenth. Gerbert, Bahr, and others gave the Passion hymn to Claudianus Mamertus of the fifth century instead.

Pimont argues the Mamertus case at length, answering critics in detail, so Mearns's claim that the ascription lacks reason seems unfair. Without its closing doxology the hymn holds ten stanzas, each of three trochaic tetrameter verses. The Roman Breviary assigns it to Passion Sunday and the weekdays to Holy Wednesday, and to the feasts of the Finding and Exaltation of the Holy Cross.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pellegrino-ro:
Pellegrino Rossi was an Italian publicist, economist, and statesman whose life ended in assassination at Rome in 1848. Born at Carrara in 1787, he studied law at Pavia and Bologna and fled to France after Murat's fall. At Geneva he taught Roman law, married a Genevese Protestant, sat on the cantonal council, and drafted the rejected Patto Rossi constitution of 1832.

Later honours took him to Paris, where he held chairs in political economy and constitutional law, joined the Academy of Moral Sciences, and became a peer of France. In 1845 he went to Rome as envoy, then ambassador, to negotiate the suppression of the Jesuits. Under Pius IX he became minister and planned a constitutional papal government with restored order. Secret societies condemned him, and he was stabbed on his way to the assembly.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pompeo-marche:
Pompeo Marchesi, a Lombard sculptor of the neoclassic school, was born at Saltrio near Milan on 7 August 1790 and died at Milan on 6 February 1858. In Rome he trained under Canova, who urged him on warmly. Milan claimed most of his working life, and for years he taught sculpture at its Academy. Marble groups and portrait busts fill much of his output.

A giant Saint Ambrose, the city's patron, counts among his first works. For the Arco della Pace, finished in 1838, he carved reliefs of Terpsichore and Venus Urania. Twelve figures of great Italian captains adorn the Castello façade he dressed. His Mater Dolorosa group in San Carlo, on which he toiled for years, ranks among his best-known pieces. Beyond Milan stand his huge Charles Emmanuel III at Novara and his Volta monument at Como.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-san-luis-poto:
San Luis Potosí, a Mexican diocese erected by Pius IX in 1854, covers its home state with a small part of Zacatecas. Its cathedral is richly decorated, and Mount Carmel church is a fine Baroque building. Before the revolution a splendid Carmelite convent with orchard and lands running 400 miles to the sea adjoined it. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia sketches a see through exile and calm.

First bishop Pedro Barajas spent most of his episcopate in exile, the second and third bishops ruled briefly, and the fourth, Ignacio Montes de Oca y Obregón, governed in quieter times. He built a large seminary where Mexicans and some students from the United States and Canada studied under a choice staff. Part of the old convent, rebuilt, now houses the Ladies of the Sacred Heart and their well-attended school.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-southern-kian:
Southern Kiang-si was a vicariate apostolic in China, separated from the northern Kiang-si mission in 1879. It was set up as its own jurisdiction. This entry follows a remote, long-neglected field where two thousand Catholics lived among ten million people. The first superior, the Lazarist Father Rouger, made his residence at Ki-ngan-fu.

Persecution runs through the story. Christian districts were pillaged in 1884. Chapels on the Kwang-tung frontier were burned in 1900, with Christians driven from their homes. Later attacks cost missionary lives. Under Rouger's successors the mission pressed on in hardship, and the entry preserves a frank record of a small Catholic presence enduring in a vast and often hostile province.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-agnes-of-a:
St. Agnes of Assisi was the younger sister of St. Clare and abbess of the Poor Ladies, born at Assisi in 1197 or 1198 and dead in 1253. This entry follows a daughter of Count Favorino Scifi and Blessed Hortulana of the Fiumi, cousin to Rufino, one of the Three Companions of St. Francis, raised between her father's city palace and his castle of Sasso Rosso on Mount Subasio.

Sixteen days after Clare left home on 18 March 1212 to follow Francis, Agnes joined her at St. Angelo in Panso, choosing poverty and penance, and her father's fury knew no bounds. He sent his brother Monaldo with armed kin to drag her back, and the entry follows her resistance into a life of leadership among the Poor Ladies.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-clare-of-a:
San Damiano's first abbess, Clare of Assisi helped found the Poor Ladies, called the Clares. Her life began in Assisi on 16 July 1194 and ended there on 11 August 1253. Tradition names her eldest daughter of Favorino Scifi, count of Sasso-Rosso, a rich man of old Roman stock. He owned a grand Assisi house and a stronghold on Mount Subasio's flank. That, at least, is the story handed down.

Her mother, Blessed Ortolana, belonged to the noble Fiumi family, conspicuous for zeal and piety. From her earliest years Clare seems endowed with the rarest virtues, devoted as a child to prayer and mortification. Passing into girlhood, her distaste for the world and yearning for a spiritual life increased. She was eighteen when St. Francis came to preach the Lenten course in San Giorgio church at Assisi, and the entry follows the flame his words kindled in her.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-francis-of:
Francis of Assisi, founder of the Franciscan order, turned a merchant's son into the Middle Ages' most loved saint. Born at Assisi in 1181 or 1182 to the cloth merchant Pietro Bernardone and Pica of Provence, he was baptized Giovanni and renamed Francesco for his father's fondness for France. Schooled by St. George's priests and by troubadour song, he lived youthfully until conversion remade him. The Catholic Encyclopedia article of 1913 dates his death at Assisi to 3 October 1226.

His short, homely, affectionate exhortations moved whole congregations, and at Camara villagers begged in a body to join him. To meet such longing he devised the Third Order of Penance, a middle state between world and cloister for those who could not leave home. Its members bore no arms, swore no oaths, and shunned lawsuits. The entry follows a preacher whose words built three orders.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-lorenzo-da:
Lorenzo of Brindisi, Capuchin preacher and linguist, was baptized Julius Caesar and preaching by six. Born at Brindisi in 1559 to Guglielmo de Rossi and Elisabetta Masella, excellent Christians, he showed precocious piety and rapid study. Barely six, he was chosen to give the Christmas sermon on the Infant Jesus to his townsfolk, in Italian custom. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death at Lisbon to 22 July 1619.

His father died when he was twelve, and he studied at Venice with St. Mark's clerics under an uncle's care. In 1575 he entered the Capuchins as Brother Lorenzo, studying philosophy and theology after profession. As general definitor from 1596 to 1602 he lived at Rome, where Clement VIII set him to instruct Jews, and his Hebrew and powerful reasoning won many to Christianity. He founded convents at Vienna, Prague, and Graz, nuclei of three provinces, and was elected vicar-general in 1602.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tametsi:
Tametsi, meaning although, opens chapter 1, session 24, of the Council of Trent, on marriage reform. That chapter held the Church's law on clandestine marriage until Easter 1908. It ruled that marriage without the parish priest or his delegate was no marriage at all. Two or three witnesses were also required. Anyone attempting such a contract was wholly incapable of contracting, and the contract was null and void.

In modified form the same rules reached the whole Church through the decree Ne temere. Secret marriages freely entered still counted as valid, unless Church rules were breached. The chapter anathematized denials of that teaching. It also rejected claims that parental consent decides validity. It required banns, a set form of consent, and entry in the parish register. Priests assisting without delegation faced instant suspension. Couples were urged to approach Penance and the Eucharist.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vicariate-apo:
Northern Shan-si is a Chinese vicariate whose faith arrived with Jesuit and Franciscan fathers in the sixteenth century. First under Peking's bishops, then erected with Shen-si as a vicariate in 1698, it gained Hu-pe and Hu-nan for a time. Was divided into northern and southern missions in June 1890.

Its darkest year was 1900, when the official Yu-hsien ordered a wholesale massacre at T'ai-yuan-fu: Vicar Apostolic Gregorio Grassi. His coadjutor Francisco Fogolla, several Franciscan fathers and a brother, seven Franciscan Sisters of Mary, native priests, and many Christians were killed. Entrusted to the Franciscans under Mgr Eugene Massi at T'ai-yuan, the vicariate counted in 1910 fifteen European fathers, sixteen native priests, twenty-four churches, 154 chapels, 269 stations, and 170 schools.

Valentine Montanar's Catholic Encyclopedia entry describes the mission district of Southern Shan-Si, set up in 1890 for some six million people. It was run by Franciscan friars. Its head, Oderic Timmer, lived at Lu-an-fu. In 1903 the mission had 21 friars from Europe, 5 local priests, 10,300 Catholics, 9,200 people learning the faith and 94 churches. A later count rose to 15,003 Catholics and 183 churches.

Southern Shen-si is a Chinese vicariate entrusted in 1885 to Rome's Seminary of Sts Peter and Paul, founded by Pius IX. Erected as a vicariate in 1887 from the prefectures of Han-chung and Singan. Its climate is damp and changeable, and its population about five million.

Under Mgr Pio Giuseppe Passerini, resident at Tcheng-kow, the mission grew markedly. In 1885 it counted two European missionaries, three native priests, thirty-two churches, two chapels, 7,700 Catholics, and a hundred catechumens. By 1910 it had sixteen European and two native priests, fifty churches, twenty-three chapels, over 11,000 Catholics, more than 6,000 catechumens, thirty-six schools, a seminary, and orphanages for boys and girls.

letters-of-ulysses-s-grant-to-his-father:
Ulysses S. Grant's letters to his father and youngest sister cover 1857 to 1878. His nephew, Jesse Grant Cramer, edited the volume in 1912. Portraits of Grant and his parents illustrate it.

A facsimile shows Grant's handwriting in a letter to his father. Jesse Root Grant, his father, appears aged sixty-nine in one portrait. The letters span Grant's lean years, war command, and presidency. Family duty and plain honesty mark his tone throughout. Readers meet the famous general as a son and brother at home. Jesse Grant, his father, was a tanner and businessman. The son's respect for him runs through every letter.
life-of-st-francis-of-assisi:
Paul Sabatier wrote this life of St. Francis of Assisi. Louise Seymour Houghton translated it into English. Scribner's Sons held the 1894 American copyright. Hodder and Stoughton published this London edition in 1919.

Sabatier dedicates the book to the people of Strasbourg. He calls it a small result beside his long endeavor. Like the widow's mite, he hopes love outweighs the offering. His Francis helped renew modern study of the saint's life. Scribner Press printed the American sheets in New York. Joachim of Fiore's Latin line serves as the book's epigraph. Houghton had translated other French works before she took up Sabatier.
myths-that-every-child-should-know-a-sel:
Hamilton Wright Mabie edited this book of classic myths for young people. Doubleday, Page issued it in New York in 1906. Blanche Ostertag drew and decorated its pages. A picture of Medeia and Jason with the Golden Fleece fronts it.

Many tales come from Hawthorne's Wonder Book and Tanglewood Tales. The Three Golden Apples opens the set. Pomegranate Seeds, the Chimaera, and the Golden Touch follow. The Gorgon's Head and the Dragon's Teeth close the sample list. Norse tales and Homer stand beside the Greek myths. Mabie chose the tales children were once expected to know by heart.
nasa-tm-19640019313-engine-integrated-se:
William J. D. Escher and Donald D. Thompson of Marshall wrote this report. It studies steering a hydrogen rocket without swinging the whole engine. The method injects gas into the exhaust jet from the side. That side push is called secondary injection side-force in the title.

The abstract calls the idea a strong alternative to gimbaling big engines. Large hydrogen engines are heavy, and swinging them takes strong gear. The report analyzes how the side injection works in detail. It also reviews past work, noting a lack of hydrogen-focused effort. Marshall had hired out a program to fill that gap with hard data.
nasa-tm-19660024081-on-the-general-pertu:
Peter Musen, of the Theoretical Division at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, wrote this paper on how planets disturb each other's paths. In a planetary system, every planet pulls on the others with gravity. Those pulls slowly shift each planet away from the simple oval orbit it would follow alone.

Musen builds a general theory of these shifts, called perturbations. He expands the change in each planet's position vector into a series. The series is arranged by powers and products of the planets' masses. That form lets astronomers compute positions step by step, including the small effects that simpler orbit math leaves out.
nasa-tm-19670009030-payload-to-mars-reco:
C. A. Wagner, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, wrote this report, issued February 1967. It answers a planner's question: how much payload can a booster place into orbit around Mars? Wagner considers both present and future booster systems, since Mars missions were then being planned years ahead.

He derives a simple method for calculating deliverable payload for named missions. The method works with arbitrary boosters and upper stage systems. Applying it, he finds present systems could put a few hundred pounds into favorable Mars orbits. Such payloads could observe conditions on and near Mars and relay the information home.
nasa-tm-19690005066-characteristics-of-c:
Frank R. Stevenson and Daniel J. Gauntner of Lewis Research Center checked carbon resistors used to measure high voltage in this report. A board of more than a thousand such resistors measured the end voltage of a large particle accelerator. True voltage values anchor each test run on such a machine.

The board was checked in place with known nuclear reactions and a magnet tool. After more than five years of hard use, its readings still matched the factory marks closely. Heat and voltage effects on resistance were also measured. Resistance fell in a straight line as voltage rose. The pair conclude such resistors and methods can be trusted for high voltage work.
nasa-tm-19690020379-a-136-mhz-ground-sta:
Ralph E. Taylor of Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this April 1969 preprint, numbered X-523-69-135, on calibrating a satellite ground station. The station's receivers work at one hundred thirty-six megahertz. Instead of test gear alone, Taylor uses celestial noise sources: radio stars whose steady hiss gives a known reference signal from the sky itself.

Chapters walk through receiver setup, system noise temperature, and threshold sensitivity step by step. Two great radio sources, Cassiopeia A and Cygnus A, anchor the method. Trials with large dishes aimed at the galactic center are reported, in eighty-five-foot and forty-foot sizes. A final method turns the same radio stars to measuring antenna gain directly, with preliminary test data included.
nasa-tm-19700028217-mda-external-mobilit:
The Space Simulation and Experiments Office at the Marshall Space Flight Center issued this test report on September 12, 1969. It evaluates external mobility aids for the MDA, the multiple docking adapter. Astronauts working outside the craft would use the aids to move and hold position along its outer hull.

The test used neutral buoyancy, floating suited subjects in water to copy weightlessness. Its goal was a human factors judgment of the full external handrail system. Subjects found the handrail system usable, the abstract reports, and every docking port and airlock could be reached. Still, more handrails in key spots, especially around the cone section, would greatly ease an astronaut's moves.
nasa-tm-19710007891-spin-exchange-in-col:
G. M. Ressler and F. G. Major of the Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this paper in January 1971. It treats spin exchange in collisions between positive helium ions. When two such ions pass, an electron spin can swap between them, and the paper computes how likely that swap is.

The quantity sought is the spin exchange cross section, a measure of the collision's effective size for this effect. Ressler and Major calculate it in the impact parameter approximation, a way of sorting passes by closeness. A variational technique supplies the interaction potential between the two ions that the exchange creates. Sections on collision theory and the exchange interaction lead into their results and conclusions.
nasa-tm-19720012071-determination-of-ang:
John S. Preisser of the Langley Research Center wrote this memorandum in March 1972, as NASA TM X-2514, on recovering flight angles from tracking data. After a test flight, engineers know a vehicle's path from radar and its attitude from onboard gyroscopes. Combining the two should give angle of attack and sideslip, the angles between the vehicle and the air it moves through.

Preisser derives the needed equations for both rolling and nonrolling body axis systems, using a roll-stabilized gyro platform as the attitude source. The method assumes a flat, nonrotating Earth, a limit stated plainly in the summary. Sample calculations based on real flight data illustrate the method. Results from the gyro approach are compared with another technique that uses onboard camera data instead.
podcast-dannyjones-YH_M0WuD9SI:
Danny Jones hosts a talk that pushes back on a popular claim about Atlantis. The claim says the lost city sits at the Eye of the Sahara, a huge ring of rock in the desert. This episode argues the match does not hold up.

The talk works through the case point by point, from the size of the rings to the age of the rock. It also asks what Plato, who first told of Atlantis, may have meant by the tale. Fans of the Sahara theory will hear the strongest doubts raised against it. The library keeps the debate as an archive record for readers on both sides.
podcast-joerogan-bhaz6vd4nSI:
Filippo Biondi is in Rogan's studio for episode 2443 of the Joe Rogan Experience, for hours of open talk. The entry preserves the full session as aired, with the guest holding forth on his own ground across a long, unscripted sitting.

Readers get the complete back-and-forth rather than a summary, which suits a show whose meaning often sits in its slow turns. The transcript is filed as the whole appearance, start to finish. The episode stands as a full record of one of the show's long-form sittings, kept for listeners who want nothing cut.
podcast-joerogan-wKZAp3jUasI:
Episode 1953 of the Joe Rogan Experience brings Duncan Trussell back for his mystic comedy hour. By this point Trussell's visits followed a beloved rhythm: jokes first, then real talk about life's biggest questions. Neither man bothers with a plan, and that is the point.

Trussell riffs on love, death, and enlightenment in his warm, wandering style. He mixes cartoon humor with sincere wonder about what it all means. Rogan laughs, shares his own views, and keeps his friend loosely on track. For the faithful, it is another hour of laughs and light from the show's favorite regular.
security-in-your-old-age-to-employees-of:
The Social Security Board in Washington issued this pamphlet in 1936 for workers in shops, mills, mines, stores, and offices. It explains the new Social Security Act, passed by Congress the year before. From November 24, 1936, the government would open a Social Security account for each worker who qualified.

Plain pages spell out who earns benefits, what must be done, and when checks begin. A worker past sixty-five who had stopped work could draw a monthly check for life, given set work in five years after 1936. Millions of workers first learned the new old-age plan from these few pages.
the-bible-douay-rheims-book-15-1-esdras-:
First Esdras, in the Douay-Rheims version, made from the Latin Vulgate and reworked by Bishop Richard Challoner between 1749 and 1752. Behind it stand a Rheims New Testament of 1582 and a Douay Old Testament of 1609 and 1610. Chapter one turns on a promise spoken by Jeremias being fulfilled. The Lord stirs the spirit of Cyrus, king of the Persians.

Cyrus makes a proclamation through his whole kingdom and puts it in writing. He declares that the God of heaven has given him all kingdoms of the earth and charged him with a task. Exile, in this opening, begins to reverse by a pagan king's decree. A proclamation, not an army, moves the history of a returning people.
the-bible-douay-rheims-book-16-2-esdras-:
Second Esdras, in a Douay-Rheims rendering from the Latin Vulgate, in Bishop Richard Challoner's revision of 1749 to 1752. Its New Testament line goes back to Rheims in 1582, its Old Testament line to Douay in 1609 and 1610. Its first words are given as the words of Nehemias, son of Helchias, in the month of Casleu in the twentieth year, at the castle of Susa.

A heading says Nehemias hears of the miserable state of his countrymen in Judea. He laments, fasts, and prays to God for their relief. Sorrow at a foreign court, rather than action in Jerusalem, opens the book. News from home weighs on a servant of a king, and prayer comes before any plan to rebuild.
the-bible-douay-rheims-book-22-proverbs-:
Proverbs, in the version of Douay-Rheims, an English rendering of the Latin Vulgate revised by Bishop Richard Challoner over 1749 to 1752. Its two parts first appeared at Rheims in 1582 and at Douay in 1609 and 1610. The opening line calls them the parables of Solomon, son of David, king of Israel.

Their purpose follows at once: to know wisdom and instruction, and to understand words of prudence. Further aims name doctrine, justice, judgment, and equity. Short sayings, not narrative, carry this book, and the first chapter states why they were gathered. A young reader is promised training in right judgment. Solomon's name lends royal weight to advice meant for daily conduct.
the-bible-douay-rheims-book-28-jeremias-:
Jeremias, in a Douay-Rheims rendering from the Latin Vulgate, in Bishop Richard Challoner's revision of 1749 to 1752. Its New Testament line goes back to Rheims in 1582, its Old Testament line to Douay in 1609 and 1610. An introduction recalls his prayers for his persecutors and a tradition that he was stoned in Egypt by Jews who had fled there.

Chapter one gives the time and calling of the prophet, his visions, and God's encouragement to him. He is named as son of Helcias, from the priests. A reluctant young prophet, set against kings and a coming ruin, stands at the centre. The book that follows joins public warning with personal grief over Jerusalem.
the-bible-douay-rheims-book-31-ezechiel-:
Ezechiel, in Douay-Rheims form, drawn from the Latin Vulgate and carried through Bishop Richard Challoner's revision, dated 1749 to 1752. An Old Testament printed at Douay in 1609 and 1610 and a New Testament printed at Rheims in 1582 lie behind the text. Chapter one is dated to a thirtieth year, in the fourth month, when the prophet was among captives by the river Chobar.

Heavens opened, he says, and he saw visions of God. A note debates whether the thirtieth year means his age or a date from a solemn covenant. Exile by a foreign river is thus the setting for sight, not despair alone. Strange images and stern messages follow, addressed to a people punished and yet still spoken to.
the-greatest-english-classic-a-study-of-: Cleland Boyd McAfee wrote The Greatest English Classic. Its subtitle is A Study of the King James Version of the Bible and Its Influence on Life and Literature. Only a Project Gutenberg header is present here. The header gives the book's title and author. It gives a date of January 1999. It carries the usual notices on copyright laws. No page of McAfee's study itself is present. His argument cannot be told from what is here.
the-lands-of-the-saracen-pictures-of-pal:
Bayard Taylor dedicated his travel volume to Washington Irving, whom he praised for reviving Saracen history and character. The twentieth edition appeared in 1863. Taylor explains that the book forms the second part of a longer series, after his journey to Central Africa.

His travels here cover Palestine, Syria, Asia Minor, Sicily, and Spain over nearly two and a half years abroad. Taylor promises his own sincere impressions even on well worn routes. Readers get letters from lands once held by Saracen rulers, written by an American author following Irving path in Spain.
the-life-and-legends-of-saint-francis-of:
Father Candide Chalippe wrote his life of Saint Francis in French, first published at Paris in 1727. Father Hilarion Duerk revised and re-edited this jubilee edition, which carries church approvals dated September 1917. A note praises the work as reliable, instructive, and rich in incidents drawn from the oldest sources.

An English version from 1852 shortened the French original, keeping three of six books and rearranging the rest for clarity. Reflections on the spiritual life appear through the narrative. Third Order members in Cleveland received the dedication of this edition. The Cleveland dedication ties the life to working devotion.
the-mummy-and-miss-nitocris-a-phantasy-o:
Reprint front matter alone is present here for George Griffith's The Mummy and Miss Nitocris, subtitled A Phantasy of the Fourth Dimension, so the novel itself does not appear. Arno Press of New York reissued the book in 1976 in its Supernatural and Occult Fiction collection, under editorial supervision by Marie Stareck. R. Reginald and Douglas Menville served as the collection's advisory editors.

The reprint was made from a copy held by the Library of the University of California, Riverside. A set ISBN is printed, and Library of Congress cataloguing data begins at the foot of the pages shown. Readers are pointed to the volume's last pages for a complete list of titles in the collection.
the-querist-containing-several-queries-p:
George Berkeley puts his economics to the public as numbered questions. The work is dated 1735. The opening queries ask whether an industrious nation was ever poor. They ask whether a well fed and lodged people can be called poor. They ask whether a wise state should encourage industry in all its members.

Berkeley next asks about the true source of wealth. He points to labor in the four elements. He asks whether money matters only as it stirs industry. Money, on that view, lets people share each other's work. The question form forces readers to answer for themselves. Students of early economics find a sharp case here. It argues for work over bullion.
